source.authors: Bytheway JP, Price CJ, Banks PB
source.title: Deadly intentions: naïve introduced foxes show rapid attraction to odour cues of an unfamiliar native prey

value: foxes investigated significantly more sand plots with bandicoot (Perameles nasuta) odour than plots with black rat (Rattus rattus) odour or clean-towel control (chi-square 7.54, df 2, exact P = 0.024); more than 80 per cent of bandicoot plots investigated after two nights versus 17 per cent (rat) and 20 per cent (control)
units: categorical (number of sand plots investigated by foxes, Pearson chi-square across three odour treatments)
method: field sand-plot assay: sand monitoring plots (2 m wide, more than 500 m apart) raked daily; a towel pegged to the plot edge, first clean (familiarisation until fox interest in the clean towel declined) then carrying body, urine and faeces odour collected overnight on 20 x 30 cm towels placed in cage traps (bandicoot or black rat), or a clean towel (control); three treatment nights; a plot scored investigated if footprint counts, changes of direction or digging at the towel showed a fox investigation on any night; other fox activity scored as incidental passing
conditions: wild-sourced: free-living introduced red foxes on about 225 km2 of agricultural land and remnant mallee woodland at Walpeup, north-western Victoria, Australia, outside the ranges of both prey species; odour donors caught in cage traps at North Head, Sydney (page does not describe their origin further); 72 plots built, 40 met the familiarisation criterion; plots analysed n = 7 bandicoot, 12 rat, 10 control; individual foxes not identified, so plots rather than foxes are the unit; same-section secondary result: rat odour plots (17 per cent) did not differ in rate from control plots (20 per cent), no separate rat versus control test printed; the authors call the lack of interest in rat odour surprising; run date not printed
where: Results, sand plot investigation by odour treatment
quote: Foxes investigated significantly more sand plots with bandicoot odours than sand plots with rat or control odours (Pearson Chi-Square X2 = 7.54, DF = 2 exact sig. (2-sided) P = 0.024, adjusted standardized residual of 2.7).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, choice of investigation at odour-bearing plots against an unscented control, with a heterospecific odour comparator; the value is limited to odour-driven plot investigation in the plot-level chi-square and is no individual-level threshold. Licence: the nature.com article page prints 'This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.' (publisher's own free full text). Byline as printed: Jenna P. Bytheway, Catherine J. Price & Peter B. Banks; Received 04 April 2016, Accepted 29 June 2016, Published 15 July 2016. Reached with the WebSearch 'wild mammals responses to scent odour field experiment camera trap OR behavioural assay Scientific Reports' (allowed_domains nature.com), which returned the nature.com article page; the WebFetch reader returns about 125 characters per chunk, and the quote is two consecutive chunks of one Results sentence. Name: Vulpes vulpes Linnaeus 1758; Mammal Diversity Database page https://www.mammaldiversity.org/taxon/1005977/ (opened) prints authority Linnaeus, 1758, order Carnivora, family Canidae, status extant. source.authors: Dickman CR, Fardell LL, Hills N
source.title: Odour-mediated Interactions Between an Apex Reptilian Predator and its Mammalian Prey

value: sand goannas excavated artificial burrows containing small-mammal body odour significantly more often than odourless control burrows in both experimental phases; digs at odour burrows numbered 80 (Rattus villosissimus, 1365 burrow-days), 88 (Sminthopsis youngsoni, 2028 burrow-days), 79 (Notomys alexis) and 203 (Pseudomys hermannsburgensis), against 7 at control burrows over 3393 burrow-days
units: categorical (burrow excavation events and burrow-days, model comparison of odour versus odourless control burrows)
method: field artificial-burrow assay: clusters of four artificial burrows at 32 to 50 sites along bases or mid-sections of sand dunes; a small ball of cotton wool bearing the body odour of one small mammal species placed at the bottom of each of three burrows, fresh cotton wool in the fourth as odourless control; phase 1 odours of N. alexis, P. hermannsburgensis and R. villosissimus (September and November 2012), phase 2 with S. youngsoni replacing R. villosissimus (September 2013, April and November 2014); digs and tracks at burrows recorded as excavation events per burrow-day
conditions: wild-sourced: free-ranging sand goannas (Varanus gouldii) in the study area; goannas in the study were captured by live trapping or hand noosing for tracking; odour donors described as 'captive or wild-caught animals' without saying which; same-paper secondary results: goanna digging at P. hermannsburgensis burrows was not significantly higher than at R. villosissimus (phase 1) or S. youngsoni (phase 2) burrows, goannas dug less at N. alexis burrows than at the others, tracks followed the same pattern (164 tracks at odour burrows versus 29 at control); the digs count is a pooled count for the whole goanna population at each cluster, not per animal; how the 3393 burrow-days divide between control and the other odours is not stated in the text I read
quote: Model results showed that V. gouldii excavated burrows containing small mammal odour significantly more often than the odourless control burrows in both phase 1 and phase 2 (Table 2, Fig. 2).
note: Classification: behavioural_response, excavation of burrows bearing prey odour against odourless control burrows in the field; the value says goannas dig at odour burrows and does not establish which compound is the cue. Licence: PDF states the article is open access under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License (publisher's own free full text; the reader returned the licence in paraphrase chunks and the full sentence was not read verbatim, so the sentence is not quoted here). Byline as printed: Christopher R. Dickman, Loren L. Fardell, Nicole Hills; citation line 'Journal of Chemical Ecology (2022) 48:401-415'; Received 21 November 2021, accepted 6 February 2022. Reached with the unfiltered WebSearch '"Odour-mediated Interactions Between an Apex Reptilian Predator and its Mammalian Prey" Varanus gouldii goanna', which returned the link.springer.com content/pdf PDF.
